sources.entry: Python: _lisp.py: Make your own Lisp interpreter_

summary.title: lisp.py
summary.one_liner: You learn how a small Lisp interpreter works by building a tokenizer, parser, and recursive eval/apply evaluator in about 150 lines of Python 2.
keywords: structure and interpretation of computer programs
how does a lisp interpreter evaluate expressions
define and begin forms in lisp
takeaways: A Lisp interpreter splits into a tokenizer, a parser that builds nested lists, and an interpreter.
eval returns the value of an expression, while apply calls functions by binding arguments in a new environment and calling eval on the body.
Special forms like lambda, if, define, and begin must be handled directly in the interpreter because their arguments need controlled evaluation order.
Built-ins such as + and print are plain Python functions stored in a base environment dictionary.
summary.summary: The author walks through a short Python 2 source file implementing a minimal Lisp interpreter, motivated by trying to understand the metacircular evaluator from Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs. The code is presented in three parts: utility functions and data-structure classes, a tokenizer and recursive parser, and an interpreter built around eval and apply. Each section has prose explaining the design choices, such as why if must be a special form and how lambda bindings are added to a copied environment. The piece ends with a short note encouraging readers to learn hard concepts by building a basic prototype.
